{"decision":"RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Nothing here is intent and no option is preferred.

ANTHONY, 2026-09-10: *"how in this design effort, that the agent has try out every tool and skill prior to updating anything about it. If you're calling the wrong tool, then why would in another project, would an agent not also do the same? This is actually a very big deal for me that we've gone back to the agent using grep and not reflow2 where appropriate."*

TWO NEAR-MATCHES WERE READ AND JUDGED DIFFERENT. `dec:idea-a-problem-in-the-users-words-should-retrieve-the-tool-that-answers-it` asks HOW a problem stated in a user's words finds its tool, and holds five options for improving retrieval; this asks HOW A RETRIEVAL FAILURE WOULD EVER REACH SOMEBODY WHO COULD FIX IT. Both open, different answer shapes, and the measurement behind this one is attached to that node as well, because it is also a third data point for it. `dec:idea-should-reflow2-serve-a-root-cause-analysis-method` is DECIDED and is about serving an RCA method; it matched on the wording of "method" and "steps" and has nothing to do with exercising a surface before changing it.

⭐ THE OBSERVATION IS AN ASYMMETRY, NOT A LAPSE. A reflow2 developer can answer any question about reflow2 by reading its Rust. A consumer agent cannot. So when the served surface fails the developer IT COSTS NOTHING — the source is one grep away — and the failure never registers as one worth filing. The same failure costs a consumer the task, with no second channel to discover the mistake. The crutch does not merely mask the defect: IT REMOVES THE FEEDBACK THAT WOULD REPORT IT. Measured 2026-09-10 — a full day changing the tool surface with every behavioural fact taken from source and `find_tools` never called; then called, and it ranked the semantic opposite of the query while omitting the right tool.

THE OPTIONS, none preferred:

(a) NOTHING. The instructions already say to search before writing and to run `find_tools` before reporting a tool missing. The failure was a session not following what was in its context. Cheapest, and IT IS THE OPTION TO BEAT — but it is also exactly what was in place on the day it failed.

(b) A WRITTEN DISCIPLINE: before changing a tool or skill, exercise it as a consumer would and record what happened. Cheap. ⚠️ AND IT IS THE STEP-② SHAPE THIS PROJECT ALREADY KNOWS GETS SKIPPED — `rule:an-issue-is-root-caused-then-pinned-by-a-test-then-fixed` says its load-bearing step is invisible when skipped, and its own originating fix skipped it. An unverifiable "I dogfooded" is worth little.

(c) A MECHANICAL GATE: a change touching a tool's description or parameters must carry a recorded exercise of it. Verifiable, unlike (b). ⚠️ Hollow to satisfy: calling a tool once with valid arguments proves nothing about whether it was FINDABLE, which is the failure that actually occurred.

(d) MEASURE THE SURFACE RATHER THAN THE AGENT. A standing check that asks `find_tools` a corpus of user-phrased questions and scores whether the right tool comes back. Turns "did you dogfood?" into a number that moves, and degrades visibly rather than silently. ⚠️ ITS TRAP WAS MEASURED ON THIS DESIGN THE SAME WEEK: whoever writes the questions writes ones the current descriptions happen to answer — a fit validated by its own fitting set, which `cap:independent-evidence` and `dec:calibration-is-an-edge` exist for, and `CALIBRATED_AGAINST` still has zero edges. The questions must come from somewhere other than the person tuning the descriptions. THE FIELD REPORTS ARE THE OBVIOUS SOURCE: hxm_program and dev_storyflow already write down what they were trying to do, in their own words, before they knew which tool to call.

(e) FIX WHAT THE MEASUREMENT FOUND AND TREAT DISCIPLINE AS SECONDARY: a behavioural invariant that changes what a call DOES must live in the description, not only in the code. `record_change` refuses to record history into a `planned` epoch and its served description mentions "planned" zero times, so a consumer learns it only by being refused. Narrowest true statement, same class as three fixes shipped this week — but it does not generalise to "the agent reached for grep".

(f) REMOVE THE CRUTCH FOR ONE PIECE OF WORK. Do one change to the tool surface with the source deliberately out of reach, as a consumer would. Produces evidence no instruction can, once rather than standing, and is the cheapest way to learn whether (b)-(d) are worth building at all.

🛑 COUNTER-ARGUMENTS, recorded beside rather than used to argue it down.

⚠️ "EVERY TOOL AND SKILL" IS LARGER THAN IT SOUNDS: 180 tools and 23 skills. Exercising all of them before any change is not a discipline anyone keeps, and a rule nobody keeps is worse than none — the project's own reason for leaving `rule:a-design-is-named-by-an-id-not-a-path` advisory. Scoped to THE TOOL BEING CHANGED it is keepable; as a sweep it is not.

⚠️ THE BUILDER'S SOURCE ACCESS IS GENUINELY USEFUL, and a rule forbidding it would slow correct work to prevent an error of attention. The problem is not that the source was read — it is that the surface was never tried FIRST, so its failure produced no signal. Any option should preserve the reading and add the trying.

⚠️ AND THE HONEST LIMIT OF ALL SIX: none makes a lexical catalogue able to tell a claim from its denial. `find_tools` ranked the negation. Every option here would have surfaced that sooner without fixing it, and whether the catalogue needs something other than bag-of-words is the question `dec:idea-embeddings-adoption` has carried since 2026-08-01.</decision>
<parameter name="rationale">A day of work on reflow2's tool surface was done entirely by reading its Rust, and find_tools — asked afterwards in a user's words — returned the semantic opposite of what was wanted while omitting the right tool. The asymmetry is the content: a consumer has only the served surface, so every gap a reflow2 session routes around by grepping is a wall for the people the tool is for, and routing around it is what stops it being found. Kept separate from the retrieval question because that asks how to make finding work and this asks how a failure to find would ever reach someone who could fix it. Recorded as an idea because the cheapest option is that the instructions already said this and were not followed, and because the most promising carries the circular-validation trap measured on this same design this week.","kind":"exploratory","name":"OPEN — should a session USE a tool as a consumer would before changing it? The builder's grep is a crutch no consumer has, so the surface can fail him for free and he never files it","status":"proposed"}
